title: Joseph weeps
hookLine: Joseph reveals himself to the brothers who sold him, and weeps (Genesis 45:1–15)

cards: Egypt, a room in the governor's house. The brothers from Canaan stand before the governor, terrified. A silver cup was found in the sack of the youngest, Benjamin, and now the governor means to keep him as a slave.
Judah steps forward and offers himself instead. He can't go home without the boy, he says; it would kill their old father. What the brothers don't know is that the governor understands every word.
He is Joseph, the brother they sold into slavery years ago. And he has just reached the end of what he can hold in.

teach.h: CAUSE EVERY MAN TO GO OUT.
teach.b: First, the room empties. In the King James words: "Then Joseph could not refrain himself before all them that stood by him; and he cried, Cause every man to go out from me."
Whatever happens next, he won't make his brothers face it in front of strangers. Second, the sound.
"And he wept aloud: and the Egyptians and the house of Pharaoh heard." Earlier he turned away from them to weep, and once hurried out to a private room. This time he doesn't hide it.
Then the plainest words: "I am Joseph your brother, whom ye sold into Egypt." He names exactly what they did. Third, what he does with it.
The brothers can't answer. So Joseph tells them not to be grieved, nor angry with themselves, and says God sent him ahead to keep people alive through the famine. Readers disagree about this.
Some hear deep forgiveness. Some notice he never says I forgive you, and that later in Genesis, after their father dies, the brothers are afraid all over again. The text lets both readings stand.
Fourth, the last line. Joseph kisses each of them and weeps on them.
Then: "and after that his brethren talked with him."
After the tears, talking. It may be the whole point: years of silence, and then a family in one room, speaking again.

how: Jews read the story of Joseph and his brothers in the weekly Torah portions in synagogue, and Christians read it in Genesis too; it is often taught as a story of reconciliation within a family.

games.q: you're Joseph. the brothers who sold you stand before you, not knowing who you are. Judah has just offered himself as a slave for Benjamin. what do you do?
o: send everyone out and tell them who you are.
games.why: Joseph can't hold it in: he sends every man out, weeps aloud so the house of Pharaoh hears, and says, "I am Joseph your brother."

practice: Bring to mind someone whose hurt is real but not the deepest one, and notice whatever rises when their face comes, in the hands or the stomach or the breath, without pushing it away.

You're not saying it was fine; like Joseph, you can name exactly what happened and still let something soften by one degree, the shoulders dropping a little. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer, just as they are.
